children.text:
Amdahl's Law [1] is not your friend here. Even a thousand women can't produce a baby in one month. Trying a million things in parallel doesn't help much when the possibilities involve cosmic-level numbers and you need to iterate on past results to make progress.

[1] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amdahl%27s_law

We already have as much parallelization as companies can afford: Hundreds, if not thousands of new corn varieties, coming from one lab. The budget is the limit. Testing is just expensive.

Process improvements come from failing faster, so you spend less money on your test. Finding the actual answer without testing would also be wonderful, but LLMs might be fast, but they aren't magic. Something like Alphafold saves time in some steps, but it's not just "hand me a candidate", but find completely novel verification mechanisms, which would be just as useful for humans. Either way, parallelization is unlikely to increase.

Specifically, it's because the verification loops are much longer in applied sciences. In biology you need to wait for wet lab experiments, clinical trials, regulatory steps, etc. before you can call something "solved".

Since sequential steps are slow, I think we're going to see massive increases in parallelization. I'm not sure how the regulatory frameworks will keep up honestly.

You can automate the setup and mechanical process. You could increase the physical capacity for parallel tests. You could increase the rate of acquiring raw materials.

But how much you cut down the time depends on how much of the trial-and-error feedback loop depends on feedback and iteration vs cast a wider initial net.

(One of the interesting things to me about the dominant software development agent pattern across all of Claude, Codex, and Cursor is that the approach is still extremely local and iterative, human-mimicking, rather than big-brain-one-shotting a novel or perfectly-fit-for-purpose software design. > Humans in a modern lab are largely unnecessary.

That is utterly untrue. It stems from the notion that biology only needs big data for us to solve all its mysteries.

Beyond that, while automated labs for cell biology are plausible and active, and the same fit organoid biology, the same really isn’t true at organism level. Labs already are artificial environments that make organisms have odd phenotypes, and odd interactions which bias the data away from what you’d find in the natural world.

You add in robotic manipulation, and you add a new confound.

Drones in the wild are an obvious counterbalance to this, though even in that scenario, the drone can be a confound unless well hidden.

In the end though, this kind of systemic breakdown of biology, while much needed raw material to improve our theories, won’t solve the whole of biology. Human hands and human minds will be needed for a good long while.

I wish there was something like LEAN for biology. But there just isn't nearly enough data to build anything close to a good drug discovery simulator. To have a LEAN for drug discovery, we would need to simulate human physiology down to the molecular interactions at a reasonable accuracy.

We currently have disparate datasets that allows us to make some predictions on how drugs will interact with molecules. And we have studies on how these molecules might affect our organs/bodies. But all of this data are at different resolutions, sparsity, and have different experimental context. It is extremely hard to reconcile for a holistic model.

DNA is the great unifier in molecular biology as it is the digital anchor/foundation that everything above relies on. But there is just so much complexity above it. An analogy in the AI space would be model distillation where you are trying to discover all the weights in a LLM by giving it a prompt and seeing what the results are. With biology, we know the prompt (DNA sequence, genotype) and we can kind of quantify the result (phenotype). And we have to figure out all the weights in between (how DNA becomes a fully functioning organism).

I wonder if this is true (I am less than a layman, so feel free to disregard).

My feeling on this is that math is amenable to LLM based development because the formalism of LEAN + the ability of AI to nudge research means that we basically have machines that can "research" through what is basically brute force search, but where the explored trees are ordered by AI.

But what if there were a biological system similar to LEAN for drug interaction? Could we not use AI in a similar way to nudge the exploration space based on the vibes that the AI has about drug discovery?

I agree there is a a distinction in the formalism of a proof (through LEAN) and the sort of probabilistic/chemical/physical/whatever nature of a biological organism (through some sort of future modeler for life science). But is the fact that one system is deterministic and the other probabilistic really as much of a leap as you think?

I appreciate you diving into the details, that's helpful to me. I've reread their post. They do say Claude many times so yes it's clear they are framing their work this way.

We have seen how these large models learn high order levels of understanding that is unexpected, e.g. physics in video generation. Hopefully that's not the case.

Well first off: molecular screening (which is basically what you're describing) is inadequate for drug discovery. There are too many other factors that matter: water positions, molecular flexibility, short and long-range electrostatics, entropy loss, coordinating ions, and more. You need not only the "pocket", but an accurate model of the system's conformational change over time, to have any hope of understanding binding energetics. It's a bigger problem for small molecule drug discovery than biologics, but it still matters.

That said, we have extremely well-refined force fields that attempt to model the underlying physics, and still fail to do this well. There's absolutely no reason to believe that a generic LLM will bring anything to the table that improves the situation. Even with the hand-wavy assertion that we (somehow) get "lots and lots of data", and somehow train a purpose-built model to do the same, it's kind of like saying that we could turn a minivan into a formula one car with enough effort. Different tools for different jobs.

I actually do believe that informatics approaches will be helpful given lots of system-specific data, but when I say that, I mean "a bespoke neural energetic model that is trained specifically for some molecular system down to customized force-field parameters", not "Claude".

So sure, maybe Anthropic will invest lots of time and money and energy into making these kinds of molecular simulation models, which they can then use for high-throughput screening experiments. But even if they do all of that, there's still no guarantee that they'll bring anything to the party that hasn't been done before...because this is the lowest-value step of drug discovery, and a model like that won't tell you if your drug is going to be toxic, or have off-target effects, or have metabolic problems, or...a million other things, which are what kill drug programs in phase 1 and beyond.

My reading of the hypothesis is this, interested in your thoughts:

> unless you can create a magical classifier

A generator could concentrate on pockets while remaining unable to judge most drugs. And LLM RLVR a) works well, and b) is black box optimisation and so is suited since it doesn't need system identification (which you can't do for complex biological systems). So the hypothesis is that, yes making a classifier is very very hard, but you could through some (lots?) initial interactive data, end up with our generator outputting with high probability drugs-that-end-up-passing-trials-with-probability-p. Whether these drugs thus generated are drugs we care about (i.e, whether `p` is good enough) and whether the whole pocket it generates in is large enough, and how jagged this behaviour is (i.e distribution of `p` across taxonomies of drugs), are the few questions we want answered.

That's all true, but they don't mention the relative costs of those different tasks, or how AI helps them.

Optimizing molecular properties of a lead is important, but ultimately not a huge source of costs. In any case, LLMs probably have as much chance of predicting outcomes as anyone else (i.e. very small).

Manufacturing is somewhat expensive, but most of the cost sits in actually creating a production process, which is not a thing LLMs can do.

Clinical trials are where most of the costs lie, but unless you can create a magical classifier that can tell me if my drug will make it past phase 3, you're not significantly bending the cost curve.

Interesting. In TFA they don't focus on that, they say:

"Developing a drug involves many varied tasks: doing early research to identify a target for a drug and the right type of drug to engage it, designing a molecule with the right properties, optimizing it to be manufactured reliably at scale, drafting the regulatory filings needed to run clinical trials, designing and administering those trials, and much more.

Our strategy to realize AI’s medical benefits is based on having AI increasingly involved in all of these tasks."

children.author: vhiremath4
children.text:
Finding and designing new drugs is a long process, but it is the least cumbersome and expensive part of the process (as opposed to human trials which run on average upwards of 4x as long and cost 10-50x as much as preclinical).

And what we need is not simply more biological phenotypical data (such as genomics, biomarkers, etc.) that we can plug into a model. We actually need that AND labeled trial outcomes, which is a challenge in and of itself because pharma companies will often hide negative trial results (which are advantageous for training the model layer) in order to exacerbate the perception of drugs that make it to market (search for "missing data phenomenon pharma"). The clinical trials are an extremely costly (and necessary) market inefficiency that leads to a bunch of bad behavior that is unfortunately self-reinforcing. I spoke on the phone with a biotech entrepreneur who told me to think of the Gavin Belson (from Silicon Valley the TV show) quote where he says "I don't know about you, but I don't want to live in a world where someone other than me makes the world a better place better than me", and to just remember that's how many people think in pharma and biotech + pharma.

Augmenting how pharma companies work is a great first step. Augmenting how candidate drugs are engineered is a good first step. But that does not change the fact that we simply do not have deterministic governing laws (as we do in physics) to understand the complete pharmacokinetics/dynamics of a drug across a large patient population. You just have to run the test. It is true that AI will help, but only as much as we have a reasonable way to predict that candidate drugs will lead to positive trial outcomes and a large market.

Note that I am not a doomer here. I think AI will have a profoundly disruptive and positive impact on the pharma industry. I'm just not sure starting with drug design alone leads to hope unless there are things happening in the background between pharma + the labs (very possible) that could lead to better trial outcomes.

children.author: estearum
children.text:
Testing a drug in a terminally ill person for something other than their illness is not going to produce meaningful data.

You misunderstand how hard it is to pull signal from a drug being put into a human body, which is why we need large numbers of people who meet extremely narrow criteria (and don't have things like a terminal cancer).

Your latter idea is a good one, and hopefully something AI will help with. As you imply: we will know empirically when it's ready because trial failure rates will trend toward zero. Today we're closer to 90% failures and not even clearly trending in the correct direction.

You're aware that, as a healthy volunteer, you could go sign up for a Phase 1 study today, right? You can even earn a pretty penny doing so.

One might argue that we have calibrated drug safety to such a high degree that the aggregate negative social impacts are far higher than the costs of side effects. Of course we don’t want another thalidomide catastrophe but I think there are large potential test groups to mine who are much less sensitive to the risks. For example, the elderly and those with terminal diagnoses. Right now we only permit drug testing in very limited cases for the latter group, and only when the treatment is related to their terminal diagnosis. I’m seeing older people taking all kinds of experimental anti-aging drugs right now, either off label, or novel. We’re not collecting any of this data empirically because what they’re doing is not legal.

Further, [we are getting much better at simulating drug interactions.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41155903/) I strongly suspect AI will offer new probabilistic models to funnel novel drugs into more targeted trials which are much more likely to succeed. If we had 90% certainty of success and high certainty of lower adverse reactions I think we could allow much less stringent human trials. That means much lower cost and much faster turn-around.
